title: Recursion & Backtracking
relevance: Interviewers and OAs use recursion/backtracking to test combinatorial search: generate-all, existence, and count over a search space, plus the pick/not-pick vs for-each-choice templates.

phases.goal: Establish what recursion is, how the call stack and recursion tree work, and the two dominant combinatorial branching templates.

must_hit.point: A recursive solution needs a base case that terminates and a recursive case that reduces the problem to smaller instances of the same problem.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states base case + recursive case; mentions solutions depending on smaller instances.

must_hit.point: Each recursive call pauses the caller and is pushed onto the call stack until the child returns; missing or wrong base cases can exhaust the stack and cause overflow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions call stack growth and stack overflow from bad/unreachable base cases.

must_hit.point: A recursion tree has one node per call; children are the recursive calls from that state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes tracing recursion via a tree of calls.

must_hit.point: Two main templates: Pick/Not-Pick (two branches include/exclude current element) and For-Each Choice (try each valid option, then undo).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both templates and when each fits (array/string vs multi-option state).

probes: What must every recursive algorithm have to terminate, and what happens on the call stack as recursion deepens?
What are the two dominant templates for exploring a combinatorial recursion tree?

hints.1: Think about how a function calling itself eventually stops, and how paused callers are stored.
hints.2: Separate base case vs recursive case, then name the two branching styles over indices vs choices.
hints.3: Base case + recursive case; call stack holds paused frames; Pick/Not-Pick and For-Each Choice (with undo).

phases.goal: Show how shared-state backtracking works and how subsequence/combination patterns are specialized.

must_hit.point: Backtracking’s core is mutate → recurse → un-mutate: share one state buffer by reference, push a choice, recurse, then pop so the buffer is clean for the next choice.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes undo/pop after recurse instead of copying path/board each call.

must_hit.point: Subsequence goals reuse the same tree: print-all collects results; print-one returns true and stops further branches; count returns 1/0 at the base and sums branch results.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains the three return-type tweaks on the same pick/not-pick skeleton.

must_hit.point: Unlimited reuse (combination sum): the Pick branch stays on the same index; Not-Pick advances the index.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States pick does not do index+1 when reuse is allowed.

must_hit.point: With duplicates, sort and at each depth skip when candidates[i] equals candidates[i-1] (and i is not the first choice at that depth); each element used once advances to i+1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions sort + same-depth duplicate skip in the for-each loop.

must_hit.point: Valid parentheses: place '(' while open < n; place ')' only while close < open; stop when length is 2*n.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the open/close count rules for generating valid strings.

probes: Walk through mutate → recurse → undo on a shared path buffer—why not copy the path every call?
How do print-all, print-one, and count differ on the same pick/not-pick tree?
For combination sum with unlimited reuse, what happens to the index on the pick branch?

hints.1: Focus on what you change before the recursive call and what you reverse after.
hints.2: Same tree, different returns: list vs early true vs sum of 1/0; reuse keeps index on pick.
hints.3: Push/pop shared buffer; print-all / short-circuit bool / sum counts; pick stays at index for reuse.

phases.goal: Contrast templates and optimizations that change correctness, asymptotics, or risk of TLE.

must_hit.point: Shared buffer with undo avoids expensive copies of paths or boards on every recursive call.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares pass-by-reference mutate/undo vs cloning state each branch.

must_hit.point: On duplicate inputs, pick/not-pick plus a set for uniqueness can TLE; prefer sorted for-each with same-depth duplicate skipping.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says set-dedup after pick/not-pick is too slow; branching-level skip is required.

must_hit.point: N-Queens: naive safety per cell is O(N); tracking columns and both diagonals with arrays reduces a safety check to O(1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions cols / row+col / row-col+n-1 (or equivalent) for O(1) checks.

must_hit.point: Word Break pure backtracking repeats suffix work exponentially; memoizing by start index yields O(n^3) time with substr costs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links repeated suffixes to memoization and cites O(n^3).

probes: When would you choose for-each-choice with duplicate skipping over pick/not-pick plus a set?
How do you make N-Queens attack checks O(1)?
Why add memoization to word-break-style partition search?

hints.1: Think about duplicates causing duplicate branches, and about repeating the same suffix.
hints.2: Compare uniqueness via set vs prune at branch; compare scanning the board vs bit/array attack sets; compare pure DFS vs memo[index].
hints.3: Sort+skip same depth (avoid TLE); cols/diag arrays O(1); memo start index → O(n^3).

phases.goal: Apply templates to classic generate / search / constraint problems and state their grounded complexities.

must_hit.point: Binary exponentiation: x^n = (x^{n/2})^2 (even) or x·(x^{n/2})^2 (odd), giving O(log n) time and O(log n) recursion depth.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States halve-exponent recurrence and O(log n) time/space.

must_hit.point: Power set / all subsequences via pick/not-pick is O(2^n · n) time (2^n subsequences, O(n) copy each) and O(n) stack/buffer space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites 2^n results and O(n) copy cost.

must_hit.point: Word Search: DFS from each matching start; mark board cell (e.g. '#') then restore; time O(m · n · 3^L) with branching factor 3 and depth L.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions in-place visit mark/undo and O(m·n·3^L).

must_hit.point: N-Queens places one queen per row; time O(N!) with O(N^2) to copy each board into the answer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Row-as-depth placement and O(N!) / board-copy cost.

must_hit.point: Palindrome partitioning: choice is the next cut; try endpoints j from i if s[i…j] is palindrome, recurse from j+1; time O(2^n · n).
Sudoku: find '.', try '1'–'9' if valid in row/col/3×3 box, recurse bool success, else restore '.'.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Empty-cell scan, digit try, validity, undo on failure.

probes: How do you generate all subsets with pick/not-pick, and what is the time complexity?
Explain Word Search backtracking including how you avoid revisiting a cell.
How would you structure N-Queens recursion and what is the time bound?

hints.1: Map the problem to generate-all, existence, or constraint satisfaction.
hints.2: Subsets: two branches per index; grid: mutate cell then four dirs; queens: one per row with attack state.
hints.3: Pick/not-pick → O(2^n · n); mark '#'/restore, O(m·n·3^L); row depth, O(N!).

tradeoffs.topic: Shared mutable state with undo vs copying path/board each call
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Pass one buffer by reference: push/mutate, recurse, pop/un-mutate. Avoids expensive copies while keeping each branch’s state correct after return.

Pick/Not-Pick fits include/exclude over an index (subsets, subsequence sum). For-Each Choice fits many options at a state (phone letters, cuts, colors) and is the natural place to skip duplicates after sorting.

tradeoffs.topic: Combination Sum II uniqueness: set after pick/not-pick vs sort + skip
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Dumping into a set after standard pick/not-pick on duplicates can TLE. Sort and, in a for-each from start, continue when i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i-1]; recurse with i+1.

tradeoffs.topic: N-Queens safety: scan board O(N) vs attack arrays O(1)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Naive per-placement scans cost O(N). Maintain cols, diag1[row+col], diag2[row-col+n-1] so a placement check is O(1), trading space for time.

tradeoffs.topic: Word Break: pure backtracking vs memoized partition
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Trying dictionary prefixes then the suffix repeats identical suffixes exponentially. Memoize by start index; with O(n) loop and O(n) substr per state, time is O(n^3).

gotchas.trap: Missing, incorrect, or unreachable base cases
gotchas.correction: Always verify base cases; otherwise recursion never stops and the call stack overflows.

gotchas.trap: Using pick/not-pick plus a set to unique Combination Sum II / duplicate subsets
gotchas.correction: That approach can TLE. Sort and skip duplicates at the same tree depth in a for-each-choice loop.

gotchas.trap: Advancing the index on Pick when elements may be reused unlimited times
gotchas.correction: On Pick, stay at the same index; only Not-Pick advances. Otherwise you forbid valid reuse.

gotchas.trap: Blind take/not-take on inputs with duplicates (e.g. [1,2,2])
gotchas.correction: Identical elements generate duplicate subsets. Sort and skip same-value siblings at a depth (i > index && nums[i] == nums[i-1]).
Only add '(' if open < n; only add ')' if close < open; finish when length is 2*n so ')' never exceeds '('.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting the undo step after exploring a branch
gotchas.correction: After recurse, pop the path char/element or restore the board/cell/color so the shared state is clean for the next choice.
